pages.title: A disturbed mixture gains a direction

blocks.text: Removing ammonia from its equilibrium mixture can encourage more ammonia to form. The composition ratio has changed, creating a temporary driving force even though the equilibrium rule at that temperature is unchanged.
Le Chatelier’s principle says an equilibrium disturbed by changed conditions shifts in a direction tending to reduce the disturbance. Comparing Q with K explains the direction more precisely.

pages.transition: Connect that ratio to the thermodynamic driving force.

pages.title: Gibbs energy connects composition and equilibrium

blocks.text: ΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q. At equilibrium ΔrG = 0 and Q = K, giving ΔrG° = −RT ln K. Combining them gives ΔrG = RT ln(Q/K). Use kelvin and consistent energy units.
For Q < K, ln(Q/K) is negative, favouring forward change. For Q > K it is positive, favouring reverse change. Thermodynamic Q and K are dimensionless activity ratios.
Actual ΔrG is zero at equilibrium; standard ΔrG° need not be zero.

pages.transition: Calculate the standard energy corresponding to a known constant.

pages.title: Worked conversion from K to energy

blocks.text: Teacher-created example: K = 100 at 300 K. Find ΔrG°. ΔrG° = −8.314 × 300 × ln 100. Since ln 100 = 4.605, the result is −11486 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −11.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
The negative standard value is consistent with product-favoured equilibrium. It does not mean every possible product-rich mixture must react forward, because actual direction also depends on Q.

pages.transition: Disturb a reactant concentration while keeping temperature fixed.

pages.title: Adding reactant lowers the quotient

blocks.text: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, Q(c) = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]). Adding H₂ initially enlarges the denominator while other concentrations remain unchanged. Q falls below K, so net forward reaction forms more HI.
K stays the same at fixed temperature. The added reactant is partly consumed until a new equilibrium satisfies that same ratio. The system need not restore every original concentration.

pages.transition: Product removal changes the ratio in a similar direction.

pages.title: Removing product can drive further conversion

blocks.text: Removing NH₃ from N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ lowers Q and favours further formation. Removing CO₂ from CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) favours decomposition while the relevant solid phases remain.
Adding more of a pure solid already present does not change its activity term. Apply concentration reasoning to variable activities rather than every mass added.
A shift is the temporary net reaction before opposing rates become equal at the new equilibrium.

pages.transition: Compression changes all gas concentrations together.

pages.title: Compression favours fewer gas coefficients

blocks.text: At constant temperature, reducing volume raises gas concentrations. If gaseous coefficients differ between sides, the numerator and denominator of Q scale differently. Net reaction favours the side with fewer gas moles.
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts right on compression: four gas coefficients become two. C(s) + CO₂(g) ⇌ 2CO(g) shifts left: one gas coefficient is favoured over two. Exclude solids from the gas count.

pages.transition: Equal gas counts and inert gases prevent a universal pressure rule.

pages.title: When raising total pressure gives no shift

blocks.text: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has two gaseous coefficients on each side. Uniform compression multiplies numerator and denominator equally, leaving Q unchanged in the ideal-gas treatment.

Adding an inert gas at constant volume raises total pressure without changing reacting-gas partial pressures, so Q is unchanged. Constant volume is essential; an addition at constant pressure can change volume instead.
When unsure, calculate the changed partial pressures and Q rather than guessing from the word pressure.

pages.transition: Temperature is different because it changes the value of K itself.

pages.title: Heating favours the endothermic direction

blocks.text: For an exothermic forward reaction, heating favours reverse change and decreases K. For an endothermic forward reaction, heating favours products and increases K. The temperature change alters the equilibrium rule.
In 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), dimerisation is exothermic. Warming favours brown NO₂; cooling favours less-coloured N₂O₄. Concentration and temperature effects must be distinguished.

pages.transition: Industrial conditions must also account for how quickly equilibrium is approached.

pages.title: Ammonia: rate and yield compete

blocks.text: Ammonia formation is exothermic and reduces gas moles. Low temperature and high pressure favour equilibrium yield, but low temperature also slows the reaction. Practical operation balances both requirements.

A catalyst helps reach equilibrium sooner but does not change K or the final equilibrium composition. Removing product can increase overall conversion by repeatedly disturbing the mixture without changing K at fixed temperature.

pages.transition: Revise which disturbances change Q and which alter K.

pages.title: Revision: distinguish ratio changes from constant changes

blocks.text: ΔrG° = −RT ln K; ΔrG = RT ln(Q/K). Concentration changes and compression can change Q at fixed temperature, leading back to the same K. Temperature changes K itself.

Compression favours fewer gas coefficients if the counts differ. Inert gas at constant volume and uniform compression with equal gas counts give no ideal-gas shift. A catalyst changes the time to equilibrium.

questions.question: Why does adding reactant not change K at fixed temperature?
questions.answer: It changes Q, after which reaction adjusts composition to recover the same temperature-dependent K.

questions.question: What does compression favour in 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄?
questions.answer: N₂O₄, the side with fewer gas coefficients.

questions.question: Does helium added at constant volume shift an ideal reacting mixture?
questions.answer: No. Reacting partial pressures and Q remain unchanged.

questions.question: How does heating affect K for an exothermic forward reaction?
questions.answer: It decreases K by favouring the endothermic reverse direction.

questions.question: Why can ΔrG° be negative at equilibrium?
questions.answer: The composition term RT ln Q can balance it; actual ΔrG, not necessarily ΔrG°, is zero.

questions.question: Why use a catalyst if equilibrium yield is unchanged?
questions.answer: It makes the equilibrium composition accessible on a useful timescale.
